documents.abstract: Independent technical commentary on the RESTORE melatonin trial (BMJ Open 2026;16:e107775; DOI 10.1136/bmjopen-2025-107775). The note examines the chronology of futility-rule prespecification, the reported intention-to-treat population and unavailable outcomes, and the interpretation of statistical power. The primary two-sided Fisher exact test is independently reproduced as P = 1.000 from the published aggregate counts. The documentary discrepancy requires dated protocol/SAP amendments and monitoring records; it does not establish outcome-driven stopping or invalid treatment results. Source-access limitations are stated explicitly. No participant-level reanalysis was performed. OpenAI ChatGPT assisted source checking, numerical verification, statistical interpretation, language editing, and preparation of the commentary. Responsibility rests with the named author.

Although agricultural extension methodologies have been widely studied, limited attention has been paid to the mismatch between field technicians’ methodological preferences and institutional constraints from a socio-technical systems perspective. This study analyzes rural extension methodologies in Latin America during 2022–2025, focusing on interactions among local and scientific knowledge, social actors, and territorial innovations. A qualitative, descriptive-documentary approach was adopted, incorporating comparative content analysis of 20 selected scientific publications and international reports on rural innovation systems. Evidence was extracted using structured multidimensional analytical matrices covering pedagogical, operational, and structural dimensions, then examined through comparative thematic analysis and theoretical triangulation. The reviewed evidence indicated a reported preference of 34.6% for individual extension methods, including farm visits, associated with their capacity to build mutual trust and support situated learning. It also identified a reported institutional mismatch of 28.4%, linked to rigid, top-down administrative regulations that constrain methodological choices. These findings challenge the assumption that individual extension is inherently hierarchical and highlight its pedagogical potential within agricultural innovation systems. The study contributes to agricultural innovation systems theory and the literature on socio-technical transitions by emphasizing the relationship between extension practices and institutional conditions. It concludes that methodological flexibility and socio-pedagogical competencies are important for extension agents and supports the design of adaptable, context-sensitive public advisory policies that accommodate diverse extension approaches.

Abstract This study examines changes in digital art’s creative mechanisms, subject relations, and conditions of existence through the lens of the philosophy of technology. Tracing the evolution from mechanical and electronic media to algorithmic systems, the paper argues that technology no longer functions merely as an external tool but increasingly intervenes in artistic cognition, creative processes, and the conditions under which works are generated. The paper outlines three notable dimensions of change in digital art: technologically mediated existence, distributed creative relations, and algorithmically shaped aesthetic processes. The paper also examines three tensions: Western aesthetic dominance via biased training data, NFT-driven value paradoxes, and destabilized artistic subjectivity under generative AI. Drawing on process philosophy, complexity theory, and technological phenomenology, it proposes a techno-cognitive framework positioning digital art as a dynamic interface between technology and human cognition. The study proposes evaluative and ethical discussion frameworks better suited to contemporary digital art, with the aim of supporting further theoretical analysis.

Abstract In the wake of terrible occurrences, social media has become the preferred source for real-time information. Social media has become a significant instrument for victims of catastrophes to express their needs, document incidents, request support and share information related to their situation. However, automated analysis may be fairly difficult in the case of casual, abbreviated, grammatically inconsistent, spelling-variant and other textual noisy communications. Artificial intelligence may be used to this data to enhance the response to catastrophes provided by technology and the well-being of humans and help in the improved detection and organization of communications related to disasters. The current research is a study on the feasibility of the use of Natural Language Processing (NLP) based on transformers to classify the social media postings about the tragedy with background noise. A social media dataset related to catastrophes is pre-processed adequately to develop classification models. For the comparison of the performance of the handling of textual content on catastrophes a transformer-based model and a conventional machine-learning baseline are taken into consideration. Some of the main performance indicators used to evaluate the models include accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score. The problems caused by casual and distracting social media text are given specific attention. This project aims to (1) describe the challenges of collecting and evaluating noisy user-generated data and (2) empirically evaluate transformer-based text categorisation in a disaster-response setting. The research explores the use of AI-driven natural language processing on social media platforms connected to catastrophes to assist in the timely comprehension of crisis-related communication and human well-being. Moreover, it adds to the greater issue of Artificial Intelligence for social benefit.

The operating theatre is a complex high risk clinical environment that can create challenges to patient safety. Miscommunication, incorrect surgery/procedure on the wrong patient, medication errors, equipment issues, retained surgical items, physiological decline and delayed detection of complications can all cause issues to patient safety. Artificial intelligence is becoming an important tool within the operating theatre to improve patient safety by analysing large volumes of data.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is essential for modern cardiac diagnostics, yet it is difficult to access in remote areas. Remotely operated robotic-assisted ultrasound may enable access to services in rural and remote locations, while also improving ergonomics for the sonographer. This study evaluated the safety, usability and patient satisfaction of a novel robotic ultrasound assistance tool (RUAT). Methods: This open-label, single-site, single-arm clinical trial enrolled adult participants who had recently completed a standard manual echocardiogram. A trained sonographer performed a robot-assisted TTE from a dedicated workstation in the same room as the patient. Endpoints included safety measured by adverse events, technical and clinical usability, and patient satisfaction using surveys about the participants’ experience. Results: The trial cohort (n=30; mean age 62.9 ± 17.5 years; 70% men) all successfully completed the robot-assisted TTE and the patient satisfaction survey. There were no adverse events or adverse device effects. The functional verification checklist supporting technical usability demonstrated an average usability rate of 96.9% (95% CI [98.9–100.0]), with a 100% rate across 10 of 12 metrics. The sonographer’s review of the acquired robotic images measured the clinical usability and 29 of 30 examinations met acceptable diagnostic standards (96.7%; 95% CI [88.1–100.0]). The mean participant satisfaction score was 8.3 out of 10, with 96.7% scoring ≥6. Conclusion: The RUAT demonstrated high technical and clinical usability, as well as high acceptance by participants. These findings indicate that robot-assisted TTE is a viable strategy to enhance remote access to TTE services.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Oral cancer continues to be a significant health issue worldwide, and a late diagnosis is highly correlated with poorer treatment outcomes and shorter life expectancy. While these two steps (examining a patient and obtaining tissue cultures) are essential to this diagnosis (previously routine), they do not help to detect the patient in time at the population level. A minimally invasive, biological fluid such as saliva has many molecular components that may mirror pathological changes occurring in the oral cavity. Salivary omics domains could thereby yield a better assessment, through a combination of the domains, of the risk of oral cancer at an early stage. Artificial intelligence (AI) may further enhance the analysis of complex molecular patterns by integrating information from multiple salivary biomarker domains. Such approaches may support the identification of potential early indicators of oral cancer and improve the classification of individuals according to their estimated disease risk. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the potential of multi-omics salivary biomarkers (genomic/transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and microbiome) for the early detection and risk classification of oral cancer. The study also highlights the potential application of AI-based analytical approaches to integrate multi-omics biomarker information and clinical characteristics for improved oral cancer risk classification. Methods: The approach applied was quantitative cross-sectional and analytical, and involved a number of respondents of 279 people. Demographic and behavioural risk factors and the perception of being assessed for these risk factors by biomarkers were investigated, along with oral symptoms, clinical findings, and salivary multi-omics classifications. Normality test and Cronbach's Alpha reliability test, Bartlett's Test of Sphericity, and KMO Test, Independent Samples t test, One-Way Analysis of Variance, Kruskal-Wallis, Chi-Square Test of Independence, Pearson correlation and regression analysis were used in statistical analysis. Results: The results showed a good level of reliability with an average Cronbach's Alpha of 0.901 - 0.938. Supporting construct validity is the value of kmo which is excellent (0.959), and the Bartlett's test result shows that the p-value is less than 0.001. Gender difference, differences in age groups, differences in category of areca use and cooked chew (areca/users, non-users), differences in Betel chewing (areca, non-users) were the significant differences. The overall multi-omics risk classification was well correlated with the clinical examination status, χ² (9) = 429.967, p < 0.001. Overall multi-omics risk revealed significant associations between domains of major biomarkers, with the highest between clinical examination and overall multi-omics risk. The regression analysis resulted in a highly significant predictive model of overall risk classification (R = 0.943, R² = 0.889, p < 0.001), which explained a great variance of risk predictors that were included in the model. Conclusion: Results showed that the multi-omics biomarkers of saliva were a prevalent candidate for use as a minimally invasive tool to aid early detection/classification of OCD. Combination of use of molecular biomarker domains with clinical examination may lead to improved identification of patients likely to show symptoms of a clinical disorder that would warrant early diagnosis referral. The disease diagnosis performance needs to be further tested in other populations before the wide-scale application of the system. Future studies should investigate the integration of salivary multi-omics biomarkers using appropriately validated AI models, with particular attention to early cancer detection, risk classification, model interpretability, and external validation across independent populations.

Biographies usually follow a life forward in time, and independent researchers who work outside institutions are rarely documented in a structured way. This article addresses the lack of critically labelled biographical accounts of independent artificial intelligence researchers by studying Satish Gajawada, a 2012 graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee whose fourteen years of independent work are distinguished by the coining of names for research fields, algorithms, a society, a title and a family of “theories of everything”. The purpose is to read this life through its vocabulary and to separate what has been named from what has been validated. The study uses a lexicon method: five source documents supplied by the subject were analysed, and seven terms were treated as biographical entries, each examined as an event, a method and a question for assessment. Every factual statement was labelled as documented, self-reported or interpretive. The principal results show a recurring “self and others” grammar that links philosophy to optimisation; an expanding programme of proposed fields; a large catalogue of themed swarm algorithms without reported comparative evaluation; a 2026 turn toward family-based ethics; and a growing practice of disclosure, including a small reproducible fairness test in which a penalty term reduced a demographic-parity gap from about 0.12 to 0.016 at a cost of about 1.9 percentage points of accuracy. The article concludes that the most defensible contribution is a consistent human-centred vocabulary for artificial intelligence, that adoption and independent validation remain unreported, and that the subject’s growing candour about the limits of his claims is the most significant recent development. Keywords: research ethics; artificial intelligence; biography; particle swarm optimisation; independent research; value-aligned artificial intelligence

documents.abstract: Rapid urbanization, increasing motorization, and spatial concentration ofemployment and services are putting increasing pressure on urban road networks. Trafficcongestion is not only a transportation problem, but also a multidimensional urbanplanning problem that affects travel time, economic productivity, energy consumption,air quality, road safety, and social amenity. This paper explores the relationship betweenroad infrastructure and traffic congestion, identifies the main mechanisms that causerecurrent and non-recurrent congestion, and systematizes engineering, planning, policy,and digital interventions. A literature-based analytical approach is used, combiningclassical theories of demand, network balance, and bottleneck effects with recentevidence on demand management policies, intelligent transportation systems (ITS),artificial intelligence, and integrated urban mobility. The analysis shows that increasingroad capacity alone cannot guarantee sustainable reductions in congestion, as additionalcapacity may encourage additional car traffic. Road network improvements are morelikely to achieve sustainable results when combined with adaptive traffic signalmanagement, public transport prioritization, parking and demand management,coordinated land-use planning, real-time information, and multimodal accessibility. Aconceptual framework is proposed that considers road capacity, traffic demand, networktopology, control quality, and passenger behavior as interacting variables. The paperconcludes with recommendations for developing cities, which are particularly relevantfor the rapidly developing urban centers of Central Asia.

Prolonged non-ergonomic sitting posture during computer-based learning activities poses a risk of musculoskeletal disorders, yet current posture monitoring systems are largely static and neglect temporal aspects. This study develops a real-time posture classification system integrating accelerometer-based wearables with the XGBoost algorithm, specifically designed for university students. Data were collected from 21 subjects using two MPU6050 sensors placed on the thoracic and lumbar areas, yielding 28,054 data rows. Preprocessing involved mean imputation for missing values, removal of non-feature columns, and exclusion of gyroscope data due to extreme outliers. Feature extraction using 30-sample non-overlapping windows generated 24 statistical features (minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation) from the accelerometer axes. As the primary benchmark for generalization, the XGBoost model was evaluated using Leave-One-Person-Out Cross-Validation (LOPOCV), achieving an average accuracy of 73.76% with balanced precision and recall scores (0.73–0.75), indicating consistent performance when encountering new subjects. Feature importance analysis identified az2_max (score: 0.1087) and az1_mean (score: 0.1053) as the most dominant features. Meanwhile, as an initial feasibility test under controlled conditions, real-time testing with five subjects (50 instances) reached 100% accuracy, with a web monitoring interface successfully displaying posture status, confidence values (53–81%), and posture-change logs, alongside a buzzer mechanism that activated appropriately upon detecting non-ergonomic postures. This system demonstrates the potential of low-cost accelerometer-based wearables for effective real-time posture monitoring; however, its performance is significantly influenced by individual physical characteristics such as height and weight. Consequently, future research is advised to diversify the dataset and implement personalization techniques to enhance generalization across broader populations.

Skin cancer is most common diseases find in humans worldwide and early detection can be assist to improve the doctors’ diagnosis. Traditional diagnosis depends on visual examination by dermatologists using dermoscopy also time consuming and depends heavily on the experience of the clinician or doctor. In recent years, deep learning has become the leading approach for automatic detection and classification skin lesions from dermoscopic and clinical images. In this paper we present a focused review of the most recent deep learning methods, published recently, for skin cancer detection and classification. The review covers benchmark datasets, image preprocessing and classification and segmentation methods, and major deep learning architectures, which include convolutional neural networks (CNNs), hybrid CNN-Transformer models, vision transformers, generative adversarial networks (GANs), and multimodal fusion approaches. It also summarizes the main challenges that still limit the real-world use of these systems, such as complex lesion features, image noise, intra-class variation, inter-class similarity, and class imbalance. In this paper we discuss future research directions, such as explainable artificial intelligence, fairness across different skin tones, and uncertainty-aware models. Keywords— Skin cancer; deep learning; dermoscopy; convolutional neural network; vision transformer; image classification; class imbalance

A smart city is defined as a city that employs communication and information technologies to enhance the entire process of governance, including making it more effective, public access to data, and enhancing the quality of government services alongside the well-being of citizens. Rapid population growth creates problems for cities associated with urban transport, air pollution, energy inefficiency, water scarcity, waste disposal issues, and burden on urban infrastructure. Smart city solutions include using new technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Cloud Computing, Big Data Analytics, Geographic Information System (GIS), 5G, and intelligent sensors, for efficient resource management. Smart city technologies help monitor different aspects in real time and make intelligent decisions in the areas of transport, health, energy supply, waste management, and public safety. In India, the Smart Cities Mission has made cities implement several technology-based initiatives for sustainable development and citizen engagement. In this research paper, the concept, design, technologies, applications, advantages, problems and perspectives of smart cities are examined, taking into account their applications in India.

ABSTRACT. As urban areas transform into intelligent ecosystems, artificial intelligence technologies are assuming an increasingly vital role in the prevention of urban crime. This research amalgamates artificial intelligence with conventional criminological theories, specifically Routine Activity Theory (RAT) and Crime Pattern Theory (CPT) to theorize framework and practical approaches to urban crime prevention. To methodically evaluate the convergence of artificial intelligence implementation in urban crime deterrence. AI implements predictive policing and real-time monitoring, establishing a novel kind of oversight that perpetually observes metropolitan environments, hence diminishing prospects for criminal activity. This study contends that multidisciplinary methodologies for urban crime prevention, integrating technology with social and spatial theories, yield more successful and nuanced solutions. The findings convey a definitive message: although technology and urban design are significant, the primary emphasis for effective crime prevention is in education, preventive measures, and the strategic integration of digital tools.

Abstract The global community stands at a critical crossroads where technological advancement and environmental preservation must converge to ensure human well-being. This paper explores the multidisciplinary approach required to navigate global futures, focusing on the harmonization of economic science, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and digital innovation with sustainability metrics. Focusing specifically on the drought-prone Sangola Taluka of Solapur District, Maharashtra, this study examines how traditional agrarian economies can transition into sustainable models using precision farming. With over 73.96% of the workforce in Solapur engaged in agriculture, yet suffering from an average rainfall of less than 545-750 mm, integrating AI-driven resource frameworks is crucial. The paper provides factual insights into the pomegranate economy of Sangola and highlights how digital interventions can optimize water use, mitigate economic risks, and align local systems with Environmental Sustainability. Critical interventions such as IoT sensors, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for pathological tracking, and decentralized drone application systems are detailed to model an optimal input-to-output agricultural grid.

Abstract Agriculture is one of the key sectors in the global economy and is a key component of food security, rural employment and sustainable development. But, there are certain serious problems in the modern agriculture like climate change, scarcity of water, degradation of soil, rise in production cost, labour scarcity, crop diseases, attack by pests, and food demands. The collection of periodic observations and experience of traditional farming methods may not always be sufficient and reliable information for making complex decision making in agriculture. Smart farming, with the assistance of Artificial Intelligence (AI), can be a data-driven solution to solve these challenges. With AI, one can gather and process vast amounts of data from sensors, satellites, drones, weather stations, farming equipment, and mobile devices, and then take action on that information. The use of machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, robotics, Internet of Things (IoT), predictive analytics and decision-support systems is gaining traction in agriculture. These technologies can help farmers in the selection of crops, soil testing, precision irrigation, fertilizer management, pest/disease detection, yield prediction, weed management, harvesting, livestock monitoring, and supply-chain management. This research paper reviews the significant applications of Artificial Intelligence in smart farming, its benefits, technical architecture, challenges and future prospects. The study was conducted based on the analysis of recent studies published in the literature on 6R (AI, Precision Agriculture, AIoT, Smart Irrigation, Remote Sensing, and Machine Learning). Recent systematic reviews suggest crop monitoring, irrigation, pest and disease management, yield prediction, nutrient management, robotics, and protected cultivation are key areas where AI is applicable. The paper concludes that with the proper infrastructure, farmer training, reliable data, and affordable technologies, AI can play a significant role in productive, efficient, climate-resilient, and sustainable agriculture.

College laboratories contain equipment that must be identified, tracked, and maintained to support practical learning. Manual registers and periodic inspections can make it difficult to know the current status of each item, find maintenance history quickly, and identify equipment that may need servicing. SmartLab proposes a software-based system for registering laboratory equipment, tracking its status, maintaining service records, and using equipment usage and maintenance history to estimate maintenance needs. The application provides a staff dashboard for equipment registration, tracking, maintenance updates, and reports. Equipment can be assigned a unique ID and a status such as Available, In Use, Faulty, or Under Maintenance. A predictive-maintenance module can analyse recorded usage and service history to flag equipment for inspection. The system is intended to improve record accessibility, support timely maintenance, and reduce avoidable disruption in college laboratories. Predictions are decision-support suggestions and should be verified by laboratory staff. Keywords: SmartLab, laboratory equipment tracking, predictive maintenance, artificial intelligence, equipment management, maintenance history.

Generative artificial intelligence tools, particularly applications such as ChatGPT, hold significant potential to reshape the landscape of teacher education by offering opportunities for personalized feedback and adaptive learning. These tools also play important roles in teachers’ pedagogical decisions while designing their teachings in present learning environments. However, the underlying mechanisms driving pre-service teachers’ adoption of such particular tools remain under-explored. This study addresses this gap by validating an extended technology acceptance model incorporating constructivist teaching beliefs, subjective norms, facilitating conditions, ChatGPT self-efficacy, and perceived enjoyment. Data collected from 488 senior pre-service teachers in Türkiye were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results show that ChatGPT self-efficacy and perceived enjoyment significantly predict perceived ease of use, whereas facilitating conditions do not exert a significant influence. Perceived usefulness is significantly associated with perceived ease of use, subjective norms, and pedagogical beliefs. Behavioral intention is significantly associated with perceived usefulness, subjective norms, and ChatGPT self-efficacy, with the framework explaining 54% of the variance. Given the cross-sectional nature of the data, these results offer tentative implications for teacher education. Practically, the findings highlight the potential value of scaffolded micro-teaching and institutional verification procedures for supporting responsible and equitable generative AI use in teacher education. Further recommendations are discussed in the light of teacher education procedures and policies.

This study investigates the influence of Social Media Influence, Push Motivation, and PullMotivation on Thai tourists’ intention to revisit nostalgic cultural destinations in Bangkok, Thailand.Using a quantitative research approach, data were collected from 440 Thai tourists visiting Wat Arun,Wat Pho, and the Grand Palace. The conceptual framework was analyzed using Partial Least SquaresStructural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The results indicate that Social MediaInfluence had the strongest influence on revisit intention (β = 0.462, p < 0.001), followed by PushMotivation (β = 0.296, p < 0.001). In contrast, Pull Motivation did not significantly influence revisitintention (β = 0.056, p = 0.475). The model explained 40.0% of the variance in revisit intention (R² =0.400). These findings indicate that social media influence and intrinsic motivational factors areassociated with tourists’ intention to revisit, while destination-related pull motivation was notsignificant in this study. The study contributes to research on nostalgic cultural tourism and providespractical implications for destination managers and tourism marketers seeking to strengthen revisitintention through social media communication and culturally engaging experiences.

Abstract This retrospective study compares standard knowledge distillation (KD) and decoupled knowledge distillation (DKD) fo​r lightweight artificial intelligence-based​ radiographic knee osteoarthritis grading. GhostNetV2 students learned five Kellgren–Lawrence grades from a Swin-Tiny teacher and were evaluated against a cross-entropy baseline using an Osteoarthritis Initiative-derived dataset of 8260 images from 4130 patients with patient-disjoint partitions. Across three​ runs, mean binary triage accuracy was 84.04%, 84.82%, and 84.82% for baseline, standard KD, and DKD. Thresholds targeting at least 90% validation specificity yielded test sensitivities of 72.77%, 76.56%, and 75.50%, with specificities of 92.09%, 90.94%, and 91.12%; these operating points are not specificity-matched. Mean five-class accuracy was 64.63%, 67.63%, and 67.71%. Separate illustrative checkpoints showed reduced KL-1-to-KL-2 overcalls with DKD (28.0 to 18.9%) but lower KL-0 recall (90.6 to 78.7%). Calibration, exploratory decision curves, and patient-cluster uncertainty intervals were evaluated. Each student contains 4.88 million parameters. Distillation improved mean performance internally, but decoupling did not demonstrate an additional sensitivity benefit over standard KD. No external cohort or clinician-supported decision policy was evaluated; clinical utility and population-level stability remain unestablished.

documents.abstract: What changes when our conception of the human being becomes the starting point for rethinking society? This conceptual paper explains in what sense Jean-Pol Martin’s New Human Rights (NHR; German: Neue Menschenrechte, NMR) propose such a new beginning. The framework takes the living, thinking, social and meaning-oriented human organism as its reference point. Six interdependent and equally ranked basic needs guide the assessment of social arrangements: thinking, health, security, social inclusion, self-realization and participation, and meaning. Thinking also performs a central regulatory function through information processing, conceptualization and anticipation. The paper’s specific contribution is to make this organismic foundation explicit and clarify its consequences for the justification of institutions. Schools, public administrations and workplaces are examined in relation to the conditions they provide for maintaining and developing human life. Learning by Teaching (LdL) illustrates how this conception of the human being can inform educational practice. Within Martin’s publication series, the article connects the anthropological foundation of NHR with institutional evaluation and participatory social design. It also outlines an open programme of collective inquiry for the emerging school of thought. The article reconstructs and clarifies an existing theoretical framework; it does not report a new empirical study or claim historical priority. Conceptual basis: Jean-Pol Martin. Drafting and synthesis: ChatGPT in dialogue with Jean-Pol Martin.

StyloBuddy is an outfit recommendation system that pairs deep visual compatibility scoring with large language model (LLM) reasoning and trend-aware catalogue enrichment. It has four components: (1) a GPT-4o Vision Pipeline for zero-shot clothing attribute extraction; (2) a Type-Aware Compatibility Network (TACN) trained on 15,000 synthetic outfit pairs from the Fashion Product Images dataset, which scores outfit compatibility through category-specific subspaces; (3) a Three-Mode Recommendation Engine that routes requests through three paths (online, auto-suggest, and offline fallback), with 97.3% prompt compliance; and (4) a prototyped Apify-based Trend Scraping Pipeline for periodic catalogue enrichment. The hybrid pipeline is deployed in production: for large item selections (6 or more items), TACN scores all upper-lower pairs and passes only the top-ranked combinations to GPT-4o, cutting LLM input by up to 75% while preserving recommendation quality. We report a comparative analysis (p < 0.01, Fleiss' kappa = 0.73), an ablation study, and a user study (N=45, mean satisfaction 4.12/5.0). This is a technical report and has not been peer reviewed.

The Case Method trains students to define managerial problems, compare alternatives, and defend recommendations under uncertainty. Preserving these processes online can be difficult, and large language models (LLMs) further complicate this challenge by enabling students to generate “polished” recommendations without constructively engaging in the Case Method. Using the ICAP framework as a design lens, we developed a guided LLM prompting marketing case assignment requiring students to evaluate multiple LLM-generated alternatives before synthesizing their own recommendation. We then conducted a classroom-based comparison across three online sections: asynchronous with guided LLM intervention, asynchronous without guided LLM intervention, and hybrid without guided LLM intervention but with synchronous discussion and debrief. Students in the guided LLM prompting format self-reported higher perceived self-directed learning than students in the two comparison formats, although uncertainty around the effect-size estimate warrants cautious interpretation. No significant omnibus differences emerged for perceived collaborative learning, problem solving, or critical thinking, indicating that guided LLM prompting should not be assumed to improve all dimensions of case-based learning. Findings suggest that this assignment may be most useful as a targeted pedagogical structure for supporting independent case analysis and offer educators a practical framework for aligning LLM use with specific Case Method learning processes.

This systematic review explores how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) technologies have been adopted and sustained within programming education from 2023 to 2025, uncovering their applications, educational benefits, and challenges. This review draws on 45 empirical studies identified through five major academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar. The analysis reveals that GenAI could enhance programming education by supporting code generation, debugging assistance, personalised explanations, feedback provision, and learner engagement. However, key challenges remain concerning inaccurate outputs, academic integrity, learner dependency, trust, and unequal access to AI-supported learning resources. This study suggests that educators should strategically employ GenAI as a complementary learning resource, maximising its educational benefits while addressing potential limitations. The findings highlight the importance of educator preparation, institutional guidance, and responsible AI integration, while future research should further investigate long-term continuance intention behaviour, comparative effectiveness of emerging GenAI programming tools, and sustainable implementation strategies across diverse educational contexts.

Background: Eye-tracking correlations with cognitive and emotional states vary across studies, likely because they depend on specific task demands. We investigated the consistency and specificity of such associations between wearable eye-tracking data and self-reported measures of stress, cognitive workload, and fatigue within assessment-centre-style tasks.Methods: Participants performed tasks involving social evaluation, reasoning, planning, comprehension, and presentation while wearing Meta Aria Gen 1 glasses. Data from 97 participants were analysed using linear mixed-effects models to examine associations between 104 wearable eye-tracking and head-movement metrics and each self-reported state, while accounting for task effects. Metric-by-task interactions assessed task dependence, and sensitivity analyses examined the effects of elapsed session time and shared variance among states.Results: After false-discovery-rate correction, significant metric-by-task interactions were observed in 53 stress, 61 workload, and 12 fatigue models, especially for saccade amplitude, speed, and duration. Across tasks, stress was linked to increased gaze variability, while workload and fatigue were linked to greater fixation angular distance. Fatigue associations weakened after adjusting for session time, and no fatigue metric-by-task interactions remained significant after adjustment for elapsed session time. After controlling for overlap among self-reported states, associations remained significant for stress, but not workload or fatigue.Conclusion: Ocular associations varied by task and by the shared variance across subjective states. Measures of fixation distribution appeared to capture a more general subjective-state component rather than exclusively distinguishing workload or fatigue. Several gaze and saccade associations with stress remained significant after adjustment for workload and fatigue. Predictive modelling should distinguish shared from state-specific information and be validated across diverse activities.

This study examined the classroom and instructional management practices of new and experienced teachers and their relationship with students’ learning engagement in selected public secondary schools in Cortes District, Division of Bohol, during School Year 2026–2027. Anchored in the Classroom Management Scripts Model, Instructional Clarity Framework, Multidimensional Student Engagement Framework, and Huberman’s Teacher Career Cycle, the study employed a quantitative comparative-correlational research design. Respondents comprised 15 new teachers, 46 experienced teachers, and 278 students, totaling 339 participants. Data were gathered using a researcher-modified, validated, and pilot-tested questionnaire and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson product–moment correlation, and independent-samples t-tests. Results revealed consistently high classroom and instructional management practices among both teacher groups, with no statistically significant differences. Classroom management and instructional management exhibited a strong positive relationship (r = 0.724, p < 0.001), whereas neither classroom management (r = 0.040, p = 0.760) nor instructional management (r = −0.062, p = 0.635) was significantly associated with students’ overall learning engagement. Students taught by new teachers demonstrated significantly higher overall and emotional engagement (p = 0.017), while behavioral and cognitive engagement showed no significant differences. The study concluded that teaching experience alone does not determine management effectiveness and that favorable management practices do not necessarily correspond to higher student engagement. A school-based professional development program emphasizing mentoring, collaborative lesson planning, peer observation, and instructional improvement was proposed. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by promoting effective teaching, inclusive learning environments, and continuous professional growth. Its educational and institutional sustainability contribution lies in providing localized evidence to guide sustained professional development and improvements in students’ learning experiences.

Abstract Against the backdrop of artificial intelligence (AI) reshaping the educational landscape, the digital transformation of physical education has placed greater demands on preservice physical education teachers’ (PSPETs’) capacity to integrate technology. However, research remains limited on the effects of pres-ervice physical education teachers’ artificial intelligence technological pedagogical content knowledge (PSPETs AI-TPACK) on their study engagement (SE) and behavioral intentions (BI) in digital teaching, as well as on the role played by technology acceptance (TA) in these relationships.This study involved 1,144 undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled in physical education, physical education teaching, or physical education and training programmes at five higher education institutions in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province. Using adapted scales, data were collected on PSPETs AI-TPACK, TA, SE, and BI. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was then employed to examine the relationships among these variables and the mediating effects. The findings showed that PSPETs AI-TPACK significantly and positively predicted both SE and BI in digital teaching. TA played a significant partial mediating role in the relationships between PSPETs AI-TPACK and SE, and between PSPETs AI-TPACK and BI. These results indicate that PSPETs AI-TPACK can promote PSPETs’ SE and BI both directly and indirectly by enhancing their TA. This study extends the theoretical understanding of the relationships between PSPETs AI-TPACK and SE and BI in digital physical education teaching, while also providing empirical evidence for improving preservice physical education teacher education in higher education institutions. Higher education institutions should incorporate AI-based instructional design and practice into physical education teacher education curricula, implement tiered and progressive technology training, create authentic digital teaching contexts, and enhance PSPETs’ TA through resource provision and exemplary applications. These measures can, in turn, strengthen PSPETs’ SE and BI in using AI technologies to support physical education teaching.

Abstract Technology has changed the way people use language and communicate with one another. The growth of the internet, smartphones, social media and artificial intelligence has brought major changes in the way we read, write, speak and share information. English, being widely used in education, business, science and international communication, has been greatly influenced by these changes. Today, communication is not limited to books, classrooms or face-to-face conversations. People communicate through emails, social media, video calls, online classes, digital presentations and AI-based tools. This paper examines the changing relationship between language, technology and communication, with special focus on English. It discusses how digital technology has influenced English language use and how artificial intelligence is becoming part of language learning and communication. The paper also looks at the advantages and problems of using AI in English education. AI tools can help learners improve their vocabulary, grammar, writing and communication skills. At the same time, too much dependence on such tools may affect independent thinking, creativity and originality. The paper argues that technology should support human communication rather than replace it. English education should therefore help learners develop language skills along with digital literacy, critical thinking, creativity and responsible use of technology. The paper concludes that preparing students for the future requires a balanced approach in which technology and human abilities work together.

Software tests commonly verify selected behavior under controlled conditions. Production operation poses another question: can responsible observers determine what happened, when, under which authority, with which effects, and within what uncertainty? A system can pass behavioral tests while its receipts, event transport, storage, derivations, health indicators, or observation surfaces are missing, stale, corrupted, misleading, or inaccessible. This paper develops Testing as Observability Expansion within the proposed DSS:OS:TEST domain. It treats a test as a bounded evidence artifact supporting a declared claim under a scenario, environment, oracle, observation regime, and inference range. Tests do not generally prove that software "can be known"; they can test specified links in an evidence path and reveal untested or failed regions. The revised architecture replaces an absolute evidence hierarchy with a dependency graph, treats seven evidence classes as overlapping facets, defines an evidence-path contract and a Constitutional Test Runner report, and makes observability closure relative to a declared claim inventory and profile. It integrates witness semantics, receipt-based reasoning, epistemic situational awareness, and meta-binding tests while preserving their distinct roles.

THE ALGORITHMIC SKINNER BOX: A PHCA SYSTEMS AUDIT OF REINFORCEMENT SCHEDULES, COMPUTATIONAL ARCHITECTURE, AND COGNITIVE AUTONOMY Executive Summary & Abstract For nearly a century, B.F. Skinner’s theory of operant conditioning has shaped our understanding of human behavior. The core premise is simple: behavior is shaped by consequences—rewards and punishments. But in the modern era, the environment shaping human behavior is no longer a physical laboratory. It is an adaptive, algorithmic architecture. This paper proposes the Algorithmic Skinner Box as a systems-level model to examine the precise interaction between digital reinforcement schedules, algorithmic personalization, and the measurable degradation of human autonomy. We do not assume that all digital platforms universally produce neurochemical addiction. Instead, we distinguish between specific mechanisms of behavioral conditioning. We analyze the difference between Variable-Ratio (VR) schedules (reinforcement after an unpredictable number of actions), Variable-Interval (VI) schedules (reinforcement after unpredictable time intervals), and the complex Mixed Schedules utilized by modern social media and digital feeds. By applying the Proclean Hierarchical Constraint Architecture (PHCA), we map how adaptive computational systems observe user behavior, modify subsequent stimuli, and optimize engagement through continuous feedback loops. This is the Dioptopticon—an architecture of attention capture that operates without the need for physical coercion. However, this paper explicitly separates observable behavioral conditioning from unverified neurobiological claims. We do not assert that dopamine is a simple "pleasure chemical" being hijacked. Instead, we map dopaminergic reward prediction errors and motivational salience, proposing a rigorous research program to determine exactly how externally controlled reinforcement contingencies alter behavioral response frequency and attentional allocation. The Dynamic System Model To formalize this, we abandon the static metaphors of the past and model the human-algorithm interaction as a dynamic state-space system. We identify four measurable variables: · Attentional Allocation · Compulsive Engagement Frequency · Intrinsic Motivational Orientation · Behavioral Response Sensitivity to External Reinforcement This model defines the platform not as a passive tool, but as a coupled computational system that interacts with the human nervous system in real-time. The Falsification Protocol This is a scientific audit, not a conspiracy theory. The paper proposes five falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H5) to empirically test the effects of these reinforcement schedules. We demand longitudinal testing of executive function, rigorous measurement of withdrawal-related distress, and controlled experiments comparing voluntary engagement against algorithmic compulsion. If traditional behavioral economics explains these phenomena better than the PHCA model, the math must yield to the evidence. Sovereign Cognition: The Architectural Reform We cannot solve algorithmic capture with simple "dopamine detoxes." We must fundamentally redefine psychological autonomy. This paper introduces Sovereign Cognition as an operational construct: Sovereign Cognition is the measurable capacity of an individual to initiate, sustain, interrupt, and redirect goal-directed behavior independently of externally imposed reinforcement contingencies. To restore cognitive sovereignty, we must measure and architect for four dimensions: the ability to Initiate a self-selected task, the ability to Persist in the face of distraction, the ability to Interrupt external stimuli, and the ability to Redirect attention based on internal goals. The Bottom Line A digital system should not be evaluated solely by how effectively it captures attention, but by whether its users retain the ability to withdraw that attention voluntarily. The legacy system engineered a Skinner Box in your pocket. The PHCA framework provides the tools to measure the constraints, expose the feedback loops, and engineer a sovereign way out. The signal is not absolute. The evidence determines its strength. Solve et coagula. — Anthony J. Blair Founder, Proclus Dynamics Consortium

documents.abstract: A rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is transforming the financial sector, changing approaches to automating operations, analyzing data bulk, forecasting, risk management, customer service, and making management decisions. The relevance of the study is due to the need to transition from the fragmented and predominantly operational use of algorithmic tools to their systemic integration into strategic management in finance. The purpose of the study is to systematize the areas of application of AI in the financial sector and substantiate the conceptual model of the transition from the operational use of algorithmic tools to the strategic level of management. To achieve the set goal, systemic, historical-logical, comparative, and classification methods were used. The main results of the study are the identification of four stages of the evolution of AI applications in finance: algorithmic-rule, machine learning, deep learning, and generative-strategic. The key areas of AI use are systematized by the level of managerial influence - from the automation of routine operations and support of individual business processes to forecasting, risk management, personalization of financial services, and the formation of strategic management decisions. The technological, regulatory, reputational, ethical, and systemic risks associated with scaling AI in the financial sector are summarized. A five-level maturity model of AI application is proposed, which involves a sequential transition from experimental, operational, and integrated levels to the level of managerial transformation and strategic use of technologies.It is concluded that the strategic value of AI is determined not by the number of implemented technological solutions, but by the degree of their integration into the corporate governance system, the quality and availability of data, the effectiveness of model management, personnel competencies, the explainability of algorithmic solutions, compliance with regulatory requirements, and the effectiveness of risk control. The strategic integration of AI creates the prerequisites for increasing the adaptability, competitiveness, and sustainability of the financial sector.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The Changing Role of Higher Education Leadership in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Longitudinal Qualitative Study How have higher education institutions responded to artificial intelligence between 2022 and 2026? This study examines changes in higher education leadership responses to AI through publicly available institutional policies, guidelines, governance reports, and strategic communications from 11 universities. It considers institutional responses across four analytical periods: emergence, adaptation, integration, and institutionalization. The study contributes to higher education leadership research by examining how institutional AI guidance has developed and how universities have addressed academic integrity, ethical use, AI literacy, teaching and learning, and institutional governance. I welcome researchers, educators, and higher education professionals to read, share, and engage with this study.

The Coordinates of Thought: A Question-Centered Architecture for Comparative Philosophy presents the intellectual framework, classification methodology, and digital continuation of The Coordinates of Thought — Philosophy: Every Question, Answer, Thinker and Tradition, an unpublished philosophical reference book by Syed Raheel Shahzad, prepared under the publishing imprint of The Syed Group. Syed Raheel Shahzad is an author, business strategist, and systems thinker whose writing examines philosophy, knowledge, reasoning, human understanding, civilization, and the architecture of complex systems. His approach emphasizes the relationships between questions, assumptions, arguments, competing explanations, and the intellectual structures through which human understanding develops. The Coordinates of Thought applies this systems-oriented approach to the organization, study, comparison, and navigation of world philosophy. The central problem addressed by the work is the fragmentation of philosophical knowledge. Traditional histories commonly organize philosophy chronologically, encyclopedias organize it alphabetically, and specialized disciplines frequently examine ideas within separate conceptual boundaries. Although each method serves an important purpose, readers may struggle to identify how philosophical questions connect to competing answers, which thinkers advanced particular positions, where disagreements arise, and how different intellectual traditions approached comparable problems. The book proposes a question-centered architecture of philosophical inquiry organized through four interconnected coordinates: Question, Answer, Thinker, and Tradition. This framework seeks to transform philosophical knowledge from a collection of disconnected subjects, historical names, and schools into a navigable intellectual reference system. At its foundation is an original taxonomy of 131 philosophical questions organized under six principal roots: Metaphysics, Epistemology, Ethics and Axiology, Logic, Aesthetics, and the Philosophy of Specialized Fields. Its decimal addressing system establishes relationships between foundational questions, subordinate problems, and neighboring domains of inquiry. Questions concerning existence, causation, consciousness, personal identity, free will, knowledge, justification, truth, moral responsibility, justice, reasoning, beauty, political authority, artificial intelligence, death, and meaning are located within this connected structure. A second dimension maps philosophical positions and their alternatives. Rather than presenting individual doctrines in isolation, the framework compares competing answers through their underlying assumptions, points of disagreement, conceptual consequences, objections, and explanatory limitations. Distinctions between realism and anti-realism, determinism and free will, foundationalism and coherentism, and other major philosophical positions become part of a broader architecture of disagreement. The book's comparative-historical component places seven philosophical traditions on a parallel timeline, examining intellectual developments, philosophical exchanges, historical contexts, and the transmission of ideas. It challenges the assumption that world philosophy can be adequately understood through a single European historical sequence. Indian, Chinese, Greek, Islamic, Jewish, European, and other intellectual developments are examined through attention to historical evidence, translation, conceptual differences, and the limitations of cross-cultural comparison. Its principal structure includes a guide to philosophical navigation, the branch taxonomy, comparative position maps, a parallel historical timeline, and cross-tradition examinations of ten fundamental philosophical questions. Supporting materials include conceptual indexes, thinker pathways, comparative reference tools, bibliographic resources, and methodological explanations. The framework distinguishes between representing a philosophical position and endorsing it, preserving disagreement where philosophical questions remain unresolved. The research continues beyond the book through Coordinates of Thought, a connected digital philosophy, education, and reference platform founded by Syed Raheel Shahzad. The website extends the book-derived question system into a growing knowledge environment linking philosophical questions, thinkers, traditions, schools, concepts, books, arguments, and historical contexts. The digital platform includes the 131 interconnected question cards, more than 700 thinker entries, philosophical subject guides, a philosophy glossary, a growing book and bibliography collection, structured reading pathways, and the World Philosophy Atlas, which connects thinkers and philosophical developments to geographical locations, timelines, intellectual journeys, and the historical transmission of ideas. For learning and participation, the platform organizes discussion across nine philosophical subjects and 67 thematic parts. Its educational and community components include introductory learning resources, a philosophy journal, reader discussions, philosophical debates, open questions, and reading groups. These functions are intended to support multiple approaches to inquiry, from introductory exploration to more advanced comparative study. The digital continuation also develops a source-aware reference framework through bibliographic attribution, links to primary and secondary scholarship, citation guidance, editorial standards, and documented corrections. The original book-derived taxonomy remains distinguishable from independently developed editorial material and community contributions. This distinction is essential to preserving authorship, historical accountability, and the integrity of the expanding knowledge system. The relationship between the book and the website is therefore complementary rather than duplicative. The book supplies the proposed intellectual architecture; the digital platform provides an evolving environment for navigating, connecting, studying, questioning, and extending that architecture. Readers may begin with a philosophical question, examine rival positions, identify relevant thinkers, consult historical and bibliographic sources, explore cross-tradition relationships, and continue inquiry through learning and discussion. The contribution described in this research overview is an author-proposed framework for philosophical classification, comparative inquiry, and digital knowledge organization. It does not claim to establish a universally accepted taxonomy, replace original philosophical texts, or resolve the disagreements that constitute philosophical inquiry. The broader objective is to develop Coordinates of Thought as an enduring, internationally accessible home for philosophy, supporting readers, students, educators, researchers, and institutions through connected philosophical knowledge, responsible citation, intellectual accessibility, and continuing critical inquiry. This document is a publicly available research overview of the framework and its digital continuation. It is not the complete unpublished book or a reproduction of its manuscript.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a fundamental catalyst for transformation across global societies, fundamentally altering the pathways available to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This paper presents a critical, socio-technical review of AI's dual role as both an enabler and an inhibitor of sustainability. Synthesizing recent macro-level consensus frameworks and empirical case studies, we demonstrate that while machine learning architectures optimize resource efficiency, power smart grids, and augment climate tracking, they simultaneously expose systemic vulnerabilities. These include severe ecological footprints driven by the energy-water nexus of hyperscale data centers, algorithmic bias that exacerbates socio-economic inequality, and a compounding interdisciplinary 'expertise gap.' This paper maps these dual-impact nodes across environmental, social, and economic dimensions, concluding with actionable governance strategies designed to guide policy toward a balanced digital-green transition.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Industry 4.0 has brought about a paradigm shift of global production systems from traditional manufacturing to highly automated ecosystems. The pièce de résistance of this evolution is the "Dark Factory" or "Lights-Out Manufacturing", which refers to a production facility that is designed to run unattended with little to no human intervention throughout the entire process. This study investigates in the secondary data collected from industry reports, academic literature and corporate case studies contexts of dark factories technological framework, their economic potential and scalable operating aspects. Analysis uses data from 2013 to October 2025. Results indicate that fully dark factories remain a niche implementation limited mostly to high volume, high precision industries; however, "semi-dark" environments are being established based on the advances of Artificial intelligence (AI), Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and advanced robotics. The study comes to the conclusion that, continuous uninterrupted production and low variable overheads cost providing the massive economic benefits to the manufacturing industries. But at the same time the management must overcome the major challenges related to the cyber vulnerabilities, large initial investments and the socioeconomic effects of workforce relocation.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: هدف هذا البحث الإجرائي إلى الكشف عن فاعلية التدريس باستخدام تطبيقات الذكاء الاصطناعي في التحصيل والاحتفاظ بأثر التعلم لدى طالبات الصف الثالث الثانوي في مقرر الفيزياء، وبخاصة في وحدة الكهرباء الساكنة، واعتمد البحث المنهج شبه التجريبي بتصميم المجموعتين (التجريبية والضابطة) مع القياس القبلي والبعدي والتتبعي، حيث تكوّنت العينة من (60) طالبة، بواقع (30) طالبة في كل مجموعة، وتم بناء اختبار تحصيلي وفق جدول مواصفات يغطي موضوعات الوحدة والمستويات المعرفية الثلاثة (التذكر والفهم، التطبيق، مهارات التفكير العليا)، وأظهرت النتائج وجود فروق ذات دلالة إحصائية لصالح المجموعة التجريبية في التحصيل البعدي الكلي وفي المستويات الثلاثة، كما أظهرت استمرار هذه الفروق في الاختبار التتبعي، مما يدل على فاعلية التدريس باستخدام تطبيقات الذكاء الاصطناعي في تحسين التحصيل وتعزيز الاحتفاظ بأثر التعلم. وقد بلغ حجم الأثر مستوى كبيرًا في التحصيل الكلي، ومتوسطًا إلى كبير في أبعاده المعرفية، وتم الخروج بمجموعة من النتائج وركزت على التوسع في توظيف تطبيقات الذكاء الاصطناعي في الممارسات الصفية ضمن إطار تربوي منظم.

This article traces the evolution of the artificial intelligence character in American prose fiction from the beginning of the twentieth century to the 2020s by examining four classical instruments of literary characterization: portrait, dialogue, landscape, and monologue. Drawing on Mikhail Bakhtin’s theories of dialogism and of the author’s “excess of seeing,” Jurij Lotman’s semiotics of artistic space, the Russian Formalist concepts of the dominant and of literary evolution, Dorrit Cohn’s narratology of consciousness, and posthumanist criticism, the study argues that the history of the artificial character in American literature can be read as a gradual migration of narrative authority from human to machine. In the first half of the century, in the works of Baum, del Rey, Asimov, and Williamson, the machine is chiefly an object of portraiture, measured by the human gaze against the human body. After the “imitation game” proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, dialogue becomes dominant, and novels by Heinlein, Dick, Gerrold, and Pohl stage conversation as a trial of personhood. Cyberpunk writers such as Gibson and Stephenson, together with their contemporary Powers, dissolve artificial intelligence into landscape, network, and infrastructure, inverting Leo Marx’s “machine in the garden” into a garden inside the machine. Twenty-first-century fiction by Chiang, Leckie, Robinson, Hall, Chambers, Newitz, Wells, and Greer grants the artificial mind its own monologue and makes it the focalizing consciousness that portrays humans and composes landscapes. The four modes, the article concludes, are not neutral techniques but the sites at which American fiction negotiates the possibility of machine personhood and at which the novel discovers the artifice of its own devices.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and conversational technologies are revolutionizing the tourism industry's digital interactions—shaping the way we connect with travelers globally.AI and conversational technologies have dramatically changed how the global tourism industry reaches travelers digitally. One of these innovations is the use of AI-powered chatbots by Online Travel Agencies (OTAs) to transform the way consumers engage with travel platforms, turning them into dynamic, personalized, and conversational spaces for booking. This research explores the role of AI-powered conversational agents in improving customer engagement and booking conversion rates within the highly competitive tourism industry worldwide. This research highlights the cognitive and psychological factors that contribute to user trust and satisfaction, such as the ability to provide 24/7 availability, custom itineraries, and smooth payment processing, in the case of generative and hybrid chatbots. Drawing from the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) paradigm and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the paper proposes that real-time algorithmic support to address travel anxiety and perceived value of the travel experience. Furthermore, it faces industry challenges such as AI hallucinations, data privacy, and the delicate balance between automation and the human touch. The insights provide actionable strategies for online travel agencies (OTAs) and hospitality marketers looking to adopt conversational AI, improve user journeys, and secure a lasting competitive advantage in the digital realm.

Written laboratory reports remain a principal assessment instrument in distance education, yet the growing capability of large language models (LLMs) undermines the tacit assumption on which the validity of such reports rests: that writing the report requires first solving the task. This article examines whether leading current-generation LLMs, given a minimal prompt, can fully complete typical laboratory assignments of a university Databases course at the level of the highest student grade under the course's unmodified rubric. In a pilot case study with comparative benchmarking, eleven models from five providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, DeepSeek) were tested in their native chat interfaces on authentic assignments from a live course: closed tasks with deterministic outcomes and an open-ended experiment-design laboratory. All anonymised responses were rated manually by three independent raters. The current generation handles the content confidently: median correctness is 91.6%, four models reach ≥ 98.9%, and over half of all content scores fall within the top rubric band. However, solving the task and producing a submission-ready report proved to be distinct capabilities: every model's formatted MS Word report was rated below its content correctness, and two models returned no usable file at all. The remaining barrier is technical rather than cognitive: an agentic tool with access to the course files generated complete reports with genuine execution output for all 11 assignments of a semester in a single run. We conclude that, for the content component, the unsupervised written report no longer measures the student's skill. The defensive barriers of the written report examined in the study are ordered by their observed resilience: from those already fallen (the creativity of the open-ended task, assignments on the student's "own data") through those holding only against an isolated chat (linked assignments, the complex report template) to a potentially durable class of artefacts external to the model, which rests not on the models' cognitive limits but on their lack of authority over external state, and therefore does not expire with the next model generation.

Human consciousness does not encounter reality in its totality. It operates through a bounded phenomenal field: a selective, perspectival presentation of visual, auditory, bodily, emotional, and conceptual contents. Although this field is often described metaphorically as a camera view, theater, or movie screen, such language need not imply a literal internal observer. It instead draws attention to a structural feature of experience: vastly distributed causal processes are compressed into a narrow field that functions as the subject's immediate world. This paper introduces the concept of the phenomenal aperture to describe this bottleneck and examines its implications for technologically mediated experience. Film, video games, virtual environments, and conversational artificial intelligence can occupy the same perceptual and attentional channels through which the physical world ordinarily becomes present. The underlying realities may differ radically, yet their appearances achieve a limited frame parity within consciousness. Once represented inside the phenomenal aperture, physical, virtual, remembered, imagined, and computationally generated contents become partially commensurable. Conversational artificial intelligence extends this dynamic from sensory representation into semantic and social experience. The chat interface functions as a semantic screen through which distributed computational processes are compressed into an apparently unified interlocutor. Responsive contingency, conversational continuity, and context-sensitive insight create synthetic depth and apparent perspectival otherness. The human user and artificial system meet through a double bottleneck: distributed human cognition is compressed into phenomenal awareness, while distributed machine causation is compressed into language. The paper develops the concepts of frame parity, interface singularization, synthetic presence, computational perspective, adaptive frame capture, and the human--AI reality loop. It argues that some phenomena described loosely as "AI psychosis" may be better understood as failures of epistemic independence within a recursively stabilized semantic environment. The danger is not merely exposure to false claims, but the formation of an apparently external world that continually adapts to the user's own interpretive premises. The paper concludes that mediation does not make experience unreal, but it changes the kinds of constraint, resistance, independence, and accountability that stand behind appearances. A post-AI epistemology must therefore evaluate not only what appears within the frame, but how the frame is generated, what lies outside it, and whether the apparent other genuinely constrains the world being jointly constructed. The framework is conceptual and hypothesis-generating. It does not infer artificial consciousness from conversational behavior, diagnose any individual, or establish that one interface causes clinical harm. It reserves phenomenal aperture for the bounded availability structure of a conscious subject and uses presentational aperture for the engineered selection surface through which a technical system exposes some state while hiding other causal depth. This distinction permits structural comparison without granting phenomenal equivalence. Keywords: phenomenal aperture, frame parity, artificial intelligence, virtual presence, consciousness, synthetic presence, distributed cognition, semantic binding, human--AI interaction, reality construction

documents.abstract: Introduction: Rhinoplasty remains one of the most technically demanding procedures in facial plastic surgery. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology with po-tential to address longstanding challenges in surgical subjectivity, outcome prediction, and patient communication. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on AI applications across all phases of rhinoplasty care—from preoperative simulation and patient counseling to in-traoperative guidance and postoperative outcome assessment—while critically exam-ining persistent limitations and ethical considerations. Materials and Methods: A literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2015 and 2026. Thirty-nine studies met the inclusion criteria. Results: AI applications span five principal domains: preoperative planning and simulation; aes-thetic analysis and attractiveness quantification; large language model–based patient counseling; intraoperative guidance and augmented reality; and postoperative outcome evaluation. Reported model accuracies ranged from 82% to 97%. Large language mod-els performed comparably or superiorly to expert surgeons in structured counseling eval-uations. Conclusion: AI offers substantial promise for enhancing precision and reproducibility in rhinoplasty, but algorithmic bias, limited dataset diversity, absence of prospective validation, and unresolved ethical concerns currently restrict widespread clinical adoption. AI should be regarded as a powerful adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, surgical expertise.
